title: Egyptian medicine into Greece
summary: Greeks credited Egypt with deep medical wisdom, and one Hippocratic jaw technique matches an older papyrus. How much they really borrowed is uncertain.
body: Greeks long treated Egypt as the home of medicine. The *Odyssey* has Helen drugging wine with a gift from Polydamna, "a woman of Egypt," a land of potent herbs where, the poet says, everyone was a skilled physician. In the late sixth century BCE the Persian king Darius sent the Egyptian priest Udjahorresnet home to re-establish the "House of Life," an old Egyptian institution of archives and learning that the Egyptologist James Henry Breasted took to include a school of medicine.

Hard evidence of borrowing is thinner than the reputation. In 1930 Breasted argued that the Hippocratic way of resetting a dislocated jaw is identical to the one in the Edwin Smith Papyrus, comparing the papyrus with a first-century BCE illustration of the Hippocratic method. A few remedies, such as the milk of a woman nursing a boy, turn up in both traditions. The closest contact came after Alexander: Herophilus taught and dissected at Alexandria under the first two Ptolemies. Whether Egyptian practice shaped what he did there is unproven.

confidence.note: That Greeks admired Egyptian medicine is plain from their own literature. Specific borrowings rest on a handful of parallels, notably Breasted's match between the papyrus and a first-century BCE illustration of the Hippocratic jaw reduction, and copying is not demonstrated. Influence on Alexandrian anatomy is plausible but undocumented.

title: Babylonian medicine into Greece
summary: Babylon had a vast, organized medical literature centuries before Hippocrates. Scholars see echoes in early Greek texts, but no route of transmission has been documented.
body: Babylonian and Assyrian healers built a large, systematic medical literature long before the Greeks: a catalogue from Assur shows that Mesopotamia had an organized corpus of medicine more than two centuries before Hippocrates. Greeks on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor lived within reach of that world, and Assyriologists such as Markham Geller have pointed to parallels between Akkadian medical texts and early Greek writings linked to the medical center of Cnidos.

A parallel is not a pedigree. The differences are deep: Babylonian medicine set out no explicit theory of humors or of hot against cold (Geller thinks its theory was implicit rather than absent), and its recipes sit beside incantations, while Greek medicine developed competing schools and theories. Geller himself stresses how Babylonian practice differed from its Greek counterpart. Influence by trade, travel or Persian-era contact is plausible, but it remains a hypothesis built on resemblances, not a documented transfer.

confidence.note: The age and scale of Mesopotamian medicine are well established from cuneiform tablets. The claim that it shaped Hippocratic medicine rests on parallels Geller noted in a few Cnidian texts, with no direct evidence of transmission, so the influence is asserted more than shown.

title: Greek medicine into Arabic
summary: In Abbasid Baghdad, translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq turned Galen and Hippocrates into Syriac and Arabic, giving Islamic medicine its Greek foundation.
body: From the middle of the eighth century to the end of the tenth, caliphs and the physician families at their courts sponsored the work of putting Greek science into Arabic in Baghdad, often by way of Syriac, the language of the Christian scholars who did much of the work. The greatest translator was Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808–873), a Christian of the Church of the East who trained in Baghdad and served the caliph al-Mutawakkil. By his own count, ten years before his death he had made 95 Syriac and 34 Arabic versions of Galen alone.

Hippocratic treatises and Dioscorides' herbal followed, in several Arabic versions. The movement did more than preserve old books. It gave Arabic a large technical vocabulary and handed Galen's humoral medicine to physicians from Spain to Iran and India, who used it as the common framework for centuries of their own writing.

confidence.note: Surviving manuscripts and Hunayn's own account of his Galen translations document the movement in unusual detail, and Arabic versions of the main Greek medical authors are well attested.

title: Indian medicine into Arabic
summary: Under the Barmakid viziers, Sanskrit classics by Charaka and Sushruta were put into Arabic and Indian physicians worked in Baghdad, a tributary later overshadowed by Greek.
body: Arabic medicine had an Indian tributary as well as a Greek one. Its patrons were the Barmakids, a family of Buddhist origin from Balkh who ran the Abbasid administration until their sudden fall in 803. Under the vizier Yahya ibn Khalid, Sanskrit classics, including the compendia of Charaka and Sushruta, were translated in Baghdad, some by way of Persian.

Later sources name an Indian physician, Manka, who came to Baghdad, treated the caliph Harun al-Rashid and stayed on to translate; Yahya is also said to have brought Indian doctors to work in a hospital he founded. A century later al-Razi was still quoting Indian authorities in his vast notebook, the *Hawi*. Much remains hazy. The best accounts come from biographers writing generations afterward, and historians admit they know relatively little about this side of the translation movement.

confidence.note: That Sanskrit medical works reached Arabic around 800 is accepted; details such as who translated what, and the Barmakid hospital, rest largely on al-Nadim's tenth-century Fihrist and similar later sources.

title: Arabic medicine into Latin
summary: From Constantine the African in Italy to Gerard of Cremona in Toledo, translators carried Arabic medicine, and the Greek medicine inside it, into Latin Europe.
body: The first major wave of Arabic medicine into Latin came from Constantine the African, who in late eleventh-century Italy turned Arabic medical books into Latin, often disguising where they came from; his versions included Hunayn's Arabic *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates. In the twelfth century the center shifted to Toledo, newly in Christian hands and rich in Arabic manuscripts. There Gerard of Cremona (d. 1187) translated al-Razi's *Book for al-Mansur*, al-Zahrawi's surgery and Ibn Sina's *Canon*.

In 1279 Faraj ben Salim, a Sicilian-Jewish physician working for Charles of Anjou, put al-Razi's enormous *Hawi* into Latin as the *Continens*. These books, and the Greek medicine they carried, became staples of European medical teaching; the *Canon* was still read at Louvain and Montpellier in the seventeenth century.

confidence.note: The translators, their texts and many manuscripts survive and are well studied; exact dates for individual translations are often approximate.

title: Indian medicine into China
summary: Buddhist monks carried Indian healing into China: tales of the physician Jivaka, formulas in his name and, by one account, needle surgery for cataract.
body: As Buddhism spread from India into China, healing traveled with it. Indian monks, one study notes, offered medical care to the poor to promote their religion. The legend of Jivaka, the Buddha's physician, survives in Chinese in several versions from the fourth and fifth centuries, one of them embedded in a monastic code. The doctor Sun Simiao later compiled formulas named after him, and a Sanskrit and Khotanese medical text attributed to him, from the ninth or tenth century, turned up at Dunhuang.

Eye surgery is the case most often cited. Couching, pushing a clouded lens out of the line of sight with a needle, is described in the *Sushruta Samhita*. A review in *Survey of Ophthalmology* says Indian monks brought it to China along the Silk Road at the end of the Western Han, though the clearest documentation is Tang: Wang Tao described the operation in 752. How far any of this reshaped mainstream Chinese medicine, rather than Buddhist circles, is unclear.

confidence.note: Indian medical material in Chinese Buddhist texts is well documented, but the early dating of couching in China rests on a single review's account, and its wider influence on Chinese medical practice is argued from scattered evidence and partly asserted.

title: Greek medicine back into Europe
summary: Byzantine manuscripts, humanist translators and the Aldine press gave Europe Galen and Hippocrates in their own Greek, and new Latin versions made from it.
body: Byzantine scholars who reached Italy around the fall of Constantinople in 1453 brought Greek manuscripts and the skill to read them. Humanist physicians wanted Greek texts they could trust: Burgundio of Pisa's medieval Latin version of Galen on hygiene, for example, had been made from an incomplete and unreliable manuscript. The Englishman Thomas Linacre, who had known the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius and studied under Niccolò Leoniceno, replaced it with a new Latin translation, first published in 1517, and went on to translate more of Galen. The Greek scholar Janus Lascaris transcribed a Galenic text from a ninth-century manuscript in Florence.

Printing made the recovery permanent. The Aldine press issued Galen's complete works in Greek in 1525 and the first Greek edition of the Hippocratic corpus in 1526. The return to the sources had an ironic result: reading the genuine Galen closely made his mistakes easier to see, and within a generation anatomists were correcting him.

confidence.note: The editions, translators and manuscripts are documented in surviving books and catalogues; how much the Greek revival, rather than new dissection, drove the later break with Galen is a matter of interpretation.

title: American remedies into Europe
summary: Guaiac, tobacco, sarsaparilla, ipecac and above all cinchona bark crossed the Atlantic, popularized by books like Nicolás Monardes's 'Joyfull newes out of the newe founde worlde'.
body: Within decades of Columbus, American plants were entering European pharmacies. Guaiac wood was shipped from America in the sixteenth century as a supposed specific for syphilis, and tobacco, sarsaparilla and curare followed. Their great publicist was the Seville physician Nicolás Monardes, who never crossed the Atlantic but grew American plants and tried them on his patients. His book, first published in Spanish in 1565, appeared in Latin in 1574 and in English in 1577 as *Joyfull newes out of the newe founde worlde*.

The most consequential import was cinchona bark from the Andes, first documented in Spanish use in Peru around 1630; although it was not part of the Inca pharmacopeia, Andean peoples seem to have used it against shivering. Shipped to Europe by the Jesuits and known as Jesuit's powder, it was used increasingly against fevers, intermittent fevers especially, which we now know to be malaria. Ipecacuanha arrived in the same century. Where Indigenous healers' knowledge lay behind these drugs, European books rarely recorded it.

confidence.note: The arrival of these drugs is well documented in printed books, but the early history of cinchona is a mixture of fact and legend; claims for many of the drugs, guaiac especially, rested on hope rather than effect, and Indigenous origins of the knowledge are usually inferred rather than recorded.

title: Ottoman inoculation into Europe
summary: Reports from Constantinople and Smyrna, and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's example, brought the Ottoman practice of smallpox inoculation to London.
body: In the Ottoman Empire, children were given a mild case of smallpox on purpose by putting matter from a smallpox sore into a small cut. In December 1713 the physician Emmanuel Timoni described the practice in a letter from Constantinople that was read to the Royal Society in May 1714; Giacomo Pylarini, a Padua-trained physician, published his own account in 1716. Timoni reported that Circassians and Georgians had brought the custom to Constantinople some forty years earlier.

The reports reached learned readers, but the practice itself came through Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, wife of the British ambassador, who watched the old women who did the "engrafting" each autumn and had her son inoculated. Back in London during an epidemic, she had her daughter inoculated in April 1721, reported as the first time it was done in Britain. That August an experiment on condemned prisoners at Newgate helped persuade the doubters. In 1722, after further trials on orphans and charity children, Princess Caroline had her own two daughters inoculated.

confidence.note: Timoni's and Pylarini's reports, Montagu's letters and the 1721–22 London trials are well documented; how much Montagu's personal example, as against the learned reports and royal patronage, changed practice is a matter of emphasis.

title: African inoculation into Boston
summary: An enslaved West African man, Onesimus, told Cotton Mather how he had been inoculated in Africa, helping set off Boston's 1721 inoculation campaign.
body: In colonial New England the decisive informant was an enslaved man. Onesimus, given to the Puritan minister Cotton Mather by his Boston congregation in 1707, told Mather he had been through an operation in Africa that gave him a mild smallpox and lifelong protection. Mather questioned other Africans in Boston and heard similar accounts, which matched what he read of Constantinople in the Royal Society's *Philosophical Transactions*.

When smallpox struck Boston in 1721, Mather pressed for inoculation, and on 26 June the physician Zabdiel Boylston began with his own son and two enslaved members of his household, a man and a boy. Boylston's figures, published in London in 1726, counted 6 deaths among 282 people inoculated against 844 among 5,759 natural cases. What is known of the African knowledge behind the experiment is recorded only through Mather's pen.

confidence.note: Mather's letters and Boylston's published account document the episode well; everything known of Onesimus himself comes from Mather, and Mather also knew the reports from Constantinople, so the African testimony was one of several spurs.

title: Greco-Islamic medicine into India
summary: Physicians at the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals brought Greco-Islamic medicine to India, where it met Ayurveda and became what is now called Unani.
body: Muslim rulers in India drew physicians trained in the Greco-Islamic tradition of Galen and Ibn Sina to their courts. Sultan Firuz Shah, who took the throne of Delhi in 1351, recorded that he had built a hospital where physicians diagnosed disease, set diets and gave medicines paid for from his endowments. At the Delhi Sultanate and later Muslim courts of central and southern India, these doctors worked alongside Ayurvedic colleagues; in 1590 the historian Muhammad Qasim Firishta described himself as a Muslim practitioner of Ayurveda. Under the Mughals the Delhi court kept drawing physicians, some of them from Persia.
The exchange ran both ways, and the tradition became Indian. The name "Unani", from the Arabic for Greek, first appears in two late eighteenth-century treatises from Delhi.

confidence.note: Court chronicles and surviving treatises document Greco-Islamic physicians in India from the Sultanate period on; how much Ayurveda and Unani actually borrowed from each other is less well studied.

title: The Indian nose job reaches Europe
summary: A 1794 report of a forehead-flap nose rebuilt near Poona inspired Joseph Carpue's 1814 operation in London, described as the first plastic surgery operation in Britain.
body: In October 1794 the *Gentleman's Magazine* printed a letter from India describing Cowasjee, a bullock driver for the British army whose nose had been cut off as a prisoner. A Maratha surgeon of the Kumar caste near Poona had built him a new one from a flap of forehead skin, shaped over a wax template; the writers said the operation was not uncommon in India and very old.

The report reached London surgeons. On 22 October 1814 Joseph Constantine Carpue, who had read the accounts from India, used the method to rebuild an army officer's nose, described by the British Library as the first plastic surgery operation in Britain, and in 1816 he published his cases. His work in turn inspired further practice by the German surgeon Carl Ferdinand von Gräfe.

confidence.note: The 1794 letter and Carpue's 1816 book survive and are explicit about the link; the claim that the Indian method descends directly from the cheek-flap operation in the Sushruta Samhita is plausible but not documented.

title: Western medicine into Japan and China
summary: Through Dutch books at Nagasaki, Japanese doctors learned European anatomy and vaccination; in China, the eye surgeon Peter Parker is remembered for introducing ether anesthesia.
body: Japan's window on Europe was the Dutch trading post at Nagasaki. In 1771 Sugita Genpaku and his colleagues took a Dutch anatomy atlas to the dissection of an executed criminal, were struck by its accuracy, and spent years translating it; *Kaitai shinsho* appeared in 1774. In 1824 the German physician Philipp Franz von Siebold opened a small school of Western medicine, and in August 1849 cowpox lymph brought by the Dutch produced Japan's first successful vaccination, which spread from Kyushu to Kyoto, Osaka and Edo within months. In 1861 the Edo vaccination clinic became the Institute of Western Medicine.
In China, the eye surgeon Peter Parker is probably best known for introducing anesthesia in the form of sulfuric ether.

confidence.note: The translations, schools and vaccination campaign are documented in surviving books and official records; the brief here covers only part of a large story, and later events such as Japan's adoption of German medicine after 1870 are not included.

title: Western medicine into colonial India
summary: Under British rule, vaccination and colonial medical schools spread through India; variolation lost official favor and indigenous medicine lost state teaching and support.
body: India already had a way of fighting smallpox: variolation had been practiced there since the early seventeenth century and was widely accepted by the time cowpox vaccine arrived. British administrators promoted vaccination in its place. In Bengal in the late 1830s a network of dispensaries supplied vaccine locally and sent lymph out with traveling vaccinators; the system was reorganized in 1853 and 1854, and the 1860s brought formal vaccination policies. Uptake was uneven. Some lower-caste Hindus welcomed vaccination partly because they had been excluded from the religious rituals around variolation.

Medical teaching changed too. In 1826 classes in Unani medicine were held at the Calcutta madrasa and in Ayurveda at the Sanskrit college. In 1835, after Macaulay's minute urged withholding grants from institutions teaching in native languages, official patronage of indigenous medicine ended, those classes were discontinued, and a new medical college trained Indian students in the European manner. Ayurvedic and Unani practitioners later built institutions of their own.

confidence.note: Vaccination campaigns and the 1835 educational decisions are documented in the cited histories; how far the colonial state actively suppressed indigenous practitioners, rather than simply ending state support, is not settled by these sources.

title: Artemisinin into world medicine
summary: A secret Chinese research project, guided by a 4th-century recipe, isolated artemisinin in 1972; in combination therapy it became the world's frontline malaria drug.
body: Tu Youyou led a research group in Project 523, a secret Chinese program launched in 1967 to find new malaria drugs. Screening traditional remedies, she returned to a recipe by Ge Hong, written about 340 CE, which took the juice of sweet wormwood (*qinghao*) with cold water rather than boiling it. That hint led to a low-temperature ether extraction: on 4 October 1971 sample 191 inhibited malaria parasites completely in rodents, and in November 1972 the team isolated crystals of the active compound, artemisinin.

The work was kept secret, and the first English-language report appeared only in December 1979. Combined with other drugs, artemisinin is now used wherever malaria is common and is estimated to cut malaria deaths by more than 20%, and by more than 30% in children. Tu shared the 2015 Nobel Prize.

confidence.note: Tu's own account and later publications document the dates, and the Nobel committee's review accepts the role of Ge Hong's recipe, which rests mainly on Tu's testimony. The project was collective, with many groups contributing, and the mortality figures are modeled estimates.

title: Rauwolfia into pharmacology
summary: Indian physicians' work on snakeroot for blood pressure and madness drew Swiss chemists to reserpine in 1952, one of the first modern blood-pressure and antipsychotic drugs.
body: The root of *Rauwolfia serpentina*, sarpagandha, was sold in Indian markets against fevers and snakebite and above all for insanity, as "drugs for the mad," though it cannot be clearly identified in classical Ayurvedic drug lists. In 1931 the Calcutta physicians Gananath Sen and Kartick Chandra Bose reported its use in high blood pressure and in "insanity with violent maniacal symptoms." In Delhi the chemist Salimuzzaman Siddiqui isolated several of its alkaloids, and in 1949 the Bombay cardiologist Rustom Jal Vakil summed up years of clinical experience in the *British Heart Journal*, bringing it to Western attention.

In 1952 Müller, Schlittler and Bein at CIBA in Basel isolated reserpine in pure form; by 1954 it was confirmed in the United States as a sedative and blood-pressure drug, and it was soon used in psychiatry. One historian argues that the Indian pioneers' part has been largely overlooked.

confidence.note: The published papers and dates are well documented, and sources name Vakil's 1949 paper as what drew Western attention; how much the Swiss work depended on the Indian research is an interpretation. The claim that rauwolfia was an ancient Ayurvedic remedy is weaker, since early-20th-century Indian researchers could not identify it in classical texts.

title: African plants into pharmacology
summary: A Calabar ordeal bean, arrow poisons and the Madagascar periwinkle gave Western medicine physostigmine, strophanthin and the anticancer drug vinblastine.
body: People of Calabar, in today's Nigeria, used the seed they called *esere* as an ordeal to judge people accused of crimes. A report by Daniell brought the bean to scientific notice in 1846; Robert Christison described its effects to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1855, and in 1864 Jobst and Hesse isolated its active alkaloid, physostigmine, later used for glaucoma and synthesized by Percy Julian in 1935. *Strophanthus* seeds, used in arrow poisons, reached European notice in the early 1860s; their action on the heart was studied by Sharpey, Pelikan and Thomas Fraser, and by about 1885 strophanthus had entered medical practice.

The Madagascar periwinkle came by a different road. In 1952 Robert Noble in Canada received leaves from Jamaica and studied them for possible anti-diabetic properties; the extract barely changed blood sugar but destroyed white blood cells. Noble and Charles Beer isolated vinblastine, patented in 1959 and made widely available with Eli Lilly.

confidence.note: The chemistry and dates are well documented; the African knowledge behind them is recorded only through European observers, and the periwinkle lead reached researchers by way of Jamaica, not from African healers.
